analysis.one_liner: Extends federal pay discrimination law to cover women and people of color in different but equivalent jobs, not just identical ones.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote; it sat in a subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to prohibit paying workers in jobs dominated by women or by people of color less than workers in jobs dominated by men or white workers, when the jobs require equivalent skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions. It would have added compensatory and punitive damages, allowed class actions and expert-fee reimbursement for workers who sue, barred employers from retaliating against workers who discuss wages, and required larger employers to report pay by sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC. The bill was introduced by DC Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, and sent to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and workers of color in jobs that pay less than equivalent jobs held predominantly by men or white workers, including those working in traditionally female-dominated occupations like care work, clerical work, and teaching-support roles. Workers would also gain protection against being fired or punished for asking about or discussing wages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and workers of color in undervalued jobs

how_it_helps.text: Under the Equal Pay Act of 1963, wage discrimination is only actionable when workers do 'equal work'; this bill would have extended the ban to 'equivalent jobs' — different jobs whose combined skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions are equivalent — covering sex, race, and national origin [S2][S3].

The bill allowed wage discrimination cases to be maintained as class actions and required courts to award expert fees to prevailing workers, making it practical for individual workers to bring claims [S2][S3].

It added compensatory and punitive damages on top of back pay, and barred employers from firing or penalizing workers for inquiring about, disclosing, or discussing their own or coworkers' wages [S3].

It required employers with 15 or more employees (25 in the first two years) to report wage rates by job classification along with employees' sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC, giving the agency and the public data on pay gaps, with confidentiality protections for individual employees [S3].
The bill prohibited employers from complying by cutting anyone's wages down — pay gaps would have to be closed upward [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with pay gaps between equivalent jobs would bear the cost of raising wages, documenting their pay systems, and submitting annual pay reports to the EEOC, plus potential back pay, compensatory and punitive damages, and class-action liability in lawsuits brought by workers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers with sex or race pay gaps

drawbacks.text: Comparing 'equivalent jobs' across dissimilar occupations — for example, a warehouse clerk versus a licensed practical nurse — is inherently difficult, and the bill would have let workers challenge an employer's stated business justification by showing a less discriminatory alternative existed, which could generate substantial litigation and unpredictable liability for employers [S3].

Employers would have faced new recordkeeping duties and annual EEOC pay reports by job classification, race, and national origin, an administrative cost falling on businesses of 15 or more employees [S3].

Critics of comparable-worth proposals have long argued that wage differences between different jobs reflect market supply and demand rather than discrimination, and that government second-guessing of occupational pay rates could misallocate labor — an objection the bill's findings section did not address directly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers paid less in equivalent jobs, the bill offered a real remedy where existing law covers only workers doing identical work. The tradeoff is genuinely contested: 'equivalent jobs' is a subjective standard that courts and the EEOC would have had to develop case by case, and the compliance and litigation costs for employers would have been significant. The bill's own guardrails — seniority, merit, production, and bona fide business-factor exemptions — narrowed its reach but also its impact.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which referred it to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2009 on April 28, 2009 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced, and on June 4, 2009 was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections [S5].
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced equivalent-jobs pay discrimination claims, class actions, and new pay-reporting duties were spared those costs. Workers in undervalued female- and minority-dominated occupations gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; no gains for affected workers

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Delegate, District of Columbia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; served on the committee to which it was referred

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. George Miller (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee on June 4, 2009 and never reported it out, scheduled a markup, or sent it to the floor

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split is recorded; the bill's only sponsor was a Democratic non-voting delegate and it drew no cosponsors from either party [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have required employers with pay gaps between equivalent jobs to raise wages, document pay systems, and file annual EEOC pay reports, with back pay, compensatory and punitive damages, and class-action exposure for violations [S2][S3]. Spared by the bill's death, these costs never materialized.

The pay-reporting requirement exempted employers with fewer than 25 employees in the first two years and 15 thereafter, so small businesses avoided the new paperwork even though the wage discrimination ban itself would have applied to FLSA-covered employers generally [S3].
Unions would have been barred from causing employers to discriminate in pay, but the bill's wage floor for equivalent jobs would also raise pay for many union members in undervalued occupations [S3].
